utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-02-54-R77.5-T, the case against Ms. Florence Hartmann.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And may we have the appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Bruce MacFarlane. I appear on behalf of the Prosecution. And with me today and throughout the proceedings is Lori Ann Wanlin to my right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Representing Ms. Florence Hartmann is my co-counsel, Guenal Mettraux, to my left, our legal assistant, Samrina Mohamad, to my right, and myself, Karim Khan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Khan. Before we proceed, I just want us to deal with one or two housekeeping matters. The parties raised a number of issues the other day at the last hearing, and two of those need to be addressed before we hear the arguments. The first matter concerns the list of questions provided to the Chamber by the Defence at the end of the hearing on the 1st of July, 2009. The Chamber reviewed these questions and found that they were far more in number and far more in scope than those which the Defence had earlier requested in their motion of the 15th June 2009. That is the response to amicus prosecutor's submission of redacted exhibits filed confidentially. In this motion, the Defence requested the Chamber to ask only three questions --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you mind slowing down. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm awfully sorry. I'll slow down. I just said in this motion, the Defence requested the Chamber to ask only three questions to the Prosecutor with respect to the work he carried out as an investigator. The Chamber would also like to refer the Defence to the Chamber's confidential decision of 17 June 2009, specifically to the bottom of page 2 and top of page 3, in which the Chamber disposed of the matter relating to the questions to the amicus investigator. The Chamber, therefore, considers that the issue has been disposed of, and the Chamber expresses its discontent with the manner in which the Defence has attempted to yet again make this request to the Chamber. The Chamber will not allow any more submissions on this matter at this stage and considers the issue disposed of. The second matter concerns the admission of a confidential Appeals Chamber decision which the Prosecution sought to tender at the hearing of the 1st of July, 2009, after the closing of its case and, indeed, after the closing of the Defence case. The Chamber notes that the Prosecution had every opportunity to tender this document with the final Defence witness during cross-examination, but did not do so. It also notes that the paragraphs which the Prosecution had indicated to the Defence were relevant to his submission were read into the transcript, and, therefore, are already part of the record of this case. Had the Prosecution wanted to rely on further paragraphs, it should have notified the Defence of this in advance. For the foregoing reasons, the Chamber decides not to admit this decision into evidence. The Chamber will now hear the final arguments, starting with the Prosecution, which has indicated it would need 30 minutes for its final arguments. The Defence shall then immediately follow and will be kept to the dead-line of 60 minutes that it was granted. The Chamber will adhere to these dead-lines strictly, as court will adjourn no later than 12.00 p.m. today. Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The case against Florence Hartmann is a relatively straightforward one. The order in lieu of indictment defines the factual issues, and the case is essentially about four critical points: Firstly, does the evidence demonstrate the actus reus in connection with what I'll refer to as the book count, "Paix et Chatiment," and the statements in some of the pages; secondly, does the evidence demonstrate a mens rea with respect to that count as well; thirdly, in connection with the article which is in issue in the order in lieu of indictment, the same two points. Is there an actus reus in respect of an offence of contempt? And, secondly, is a guilty intention or a guilty mind, the mens rea, demonstrated in connection with that count as well. Those are the four critical issues. Throughout the proceedings, there have been various, I'll call them off-ramps, largely attempts to discredit those involved in the proceedings; we're past that. And at issue right now is the merits of the case and the merits of the evidence and whether or not the evidence establishes guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. The evidence, when taken as a whole, demonstrates that the publications in question, the book and the article, were not an accident, they were not through inadvertence. The writings were deliberate, and the writings were willful. And, most importantly, the writings were all the words of the accused. It's my respectful submission that at the end of the evidence, this Chamber will be satisfied that the accused's statements were one of public defiance. I intend to deal briefly with the law, only briefly, because the Chamber is well familiar with the law concerning contempt. And I should also mention, and I will mention a few more times throughout my submission, that attached to the written argument which was filed last night in Annex A and Annex B is a line-by-line analysis of the publications in question and their linkage to the order in lieu of indictment. So that is a detailed line-by-line analysis of both the book and the article. First of all, in terms of the law, the accused, of course, has been charged with two counts of contempt of the Tribunal under Rule 77 and as well pursuant to the inherent power of the Chamber. The language of the Rule demonstrates that a violation of a court order, as such, constitutes an interference with the Tribunal's administration of justice, and as well the jurisprudence of the Tribunal establishes that it is sufficient to demonstrate a relevant actus reus and mens rea component. And the leading case is Jovic, a decision of the Appeals Chamber in 2006, and I'll be referring to that case on a couple of points. It's my respectful submission that that is the leading case for the purposes of these proceedings, and on some points it's dispositive. In terms of the actus reus in connection with the offence, the jurisprudence generally looks to the physical act of disclosure of the information relating to the proceedings to determine if the disclosure was in violation of an order of the Chamber. And it's my respectful submission that in both instances, that is, the book count and the article count, that the evidence is clear that there is a physical act of disclosure of information relating to proceedings where such disclosure would be in violation of an order of the Chamber. In connection with the mens rea component of the offence, it is clear, based on the case law, that there are at least two forms of mens rea in contempt cases that are sufficient. The one is actual knowledge that the publication was in violation of an order, and, secondly, willful blindness to that issue. So there's twin -- there's twin versions of mens rea. And in my respectful submission, the evidence is capable of supporting both or either, actual knowledge or willful blindness. I'd like to move to the four key elements and spend a little bit of time on them, because at the end of the day that's, in my submission, what the Chamber ought to focus on is those four key elements. Key element number 1, the actus reus concerning the book count. The evidence is clear that she is the sole author of the book, published by Flammarion in September of 2007. The Defence has formally admitted that the book was written by her. And in the suspect interview, she conceded that she had written the book alone. In the book, at pages 120 to 122, the accused makes express reference to the existence of two confidential decisions, as well as their contents and the purported effect of those confidential decisions. And as well at page 122, the accused actually makes express reference to the fact that those two decisions were confidential in nature. So in terms of the actus reus on the book count, there can, in my respectful submission, be no doubt that that has been established beyond a reasonable doubt. The second critical element, the actus reus concerning the article. The article was written four months after the book was published. It is entitled "Vital Genocide Documents Concealed," and the accused wrote the article herself, and it was published on-line by the Bosnian Institute on the 21st of January, 2008. During the interview, the accused conceded that she had written the article, that it was accurate, and that it was intended to be an English summary of relevant parts of the book. Moving to the third critical element, both of which deal with the concept of mens rea. The evidence, in my respectful submission, establishes a finding of actual knowledge on the book count. At page 122 of the book, the accused wrote that the Judges had rendered each of their decisions marked "Confidential." During the suspect interview, she conceded that no media release had been issued in relation to one of the decisions, "because it was a confidential decision." Two points can be inferred from these statements: First, the disclosure was not an accident, but was deliberate; and, secondly, the accused had knowledge of the existence of the order which is rendered confidential. As well, there's contextual information that needs to be considered in relation to the issue of the mens rea on the book count. The accused had worked over 20 years as a journalist, where the verification, as she indicated, of one's sources is important to maintain one's reputation and credibility. The accused, in the suspect interview, indicated that journalistic sources had assisted her in piecing the story together and that she had been told that they were confidential. She accepted that and put that in her book. In addition to that, and of significance, the accused worked in this Tribunal for six years, in a clear environment of confidentiality. No one in a senior position in this building can escape without knowing that confidentiality is important, and that was her environment. She indicated that, and it's been conceded, that she was aware of the existence of Rule 77. And during the interview she indicated that she was aware of investigations against other journalists for suspected violations. When all of that evidence is considered together, only a willfully blind or recklessly indifferent individual would not have a suspicion or realisation that an order may exist. So, once again, the mens rea, based on the evidence, can satisfy either actual knowledge or willful blindness. In my respectful submission, it's primarily actual knowledge by virtue of her statements in the book. And I'm now referring to the third critical element. The fourth and final critical element concerns the mens rea in respect of the article count. I submit as well, in connection with the article count, that the evidence supports a finding of actual knowledge. In the book which she had had published four months earlier, she noted that the decisions were confidential. She doesn't say that in the article, but her statements in the book are tantamount to a public admission, and on that basis are admissible on both counts, that is, the book count and the article count. Once again, the accused worked in that environment of confidentiality within the Tribunal, and that has to be taken into account on the fourth and final element; that is, the article count. But in addition, there's one further point that arises uniquely in connection with the article count and the fourth element, namely, mens rea, and that was in between the publication of the book and the publication of the article, the accused received a letter from the Registrar. The letter was a warning to her that the book had contained confidential information. So what happened was she received the letter and decided to go ahead anyway. All that she really did was she eliminated a reference to the fact that the decisions were rendered confidentially. But aside from that, the article is essentially the same as in the book. The point is she made a conscious decision to proceed and publish, even in the face of that warning from the Registrar. So as of the date of receiving that letter in October, the accused was fixed with knowledge that there was a live issue, and decided to proceed anyway. There are two parts of the Prosecution's case that I would like to comment on, in terms of probative value, because at this stage, while both have been admitted, weight and probative value are live issues before the Chamber. The two areas of the Prosecution's case are the suspect interview and the letter from the Registrar, and I'll try to keep this brief because I really already commented on both. But as the Chamber will be well aware, a pre-indictment suspect interview is often quite helpful, in terms of understanding what was in the mind of the accused at the time. The accused, during the suspect interview, indicated that she was alive to the sensitivity of confidential information when she was employed, but she was often not privy to the contents of confidential decisions, but that she took care, when she was spokesperson - that's the key - when she was the spokesperson, she took care to ensure that confidential information was protected. What she said was this: "My replies were given in consultation with the Office of the Prosecutor, so, in general, we knew what questions were coming at us and prepared for them. I knew exactly what the framework of my replies would be, without taking the risk of infringing upon any decisions, and you can see for yourself that such problems never arose during my period in office." So she knew about the need for care, she did take care, and she was proud of the fact that for six years she ensured that there were no problems in terms of the disclosure of confidential information. So what happened? Did all of that knowledge all of a sudden disappear when she returned to be a journalist? She knew the rules of the game. She had worked within the rules of the game for six years. And as Mr. Ruxton noted in his jointly-agreed-upon evidence, he confirmed that Ms. Hartmann was very much aware of the need for care when he said: "It was an essential part of the spokesperson's job to know what information was confidential or could not be given to the media or the public." In the suspect interview, the accused also discussed the writing of the book. She said it was started in January of 2007, after leaving the Tribunal, and was published in September of 2007. She confirmed, as I mentioned earlier, she did it alone, and it was essentially a reconstruction of events based on her own experiences and information provided by a number of unnamed sources, but it was a reconstruction. And in terms of the critical issue, it is evidence she was told the decisions were confidential, she accepted that and decided to write about it. And to note that very fact, when confronted with the confidential decisions in question, her response was, Well, it appeared I had good sources. When she was asked if there was any media releases issued at the time, as spokesperson, she said, No, I don't think so, because it was a confidential decision. In terms of the interview as a whole, it's my submission that all of the safe-guards were in place, the accused had an opportunity to set out her perspective, and it's my submission that on all of the essential elements, the interview itself establishes the offence, including the mens rea on both counts. With respect to the Registrar's warning letter, just a couple of brief comments. As I noted earlier, it was sandwiched in between the two publications. As of that date, if not earlier, the Chamber is entitled to find that she was fixed with knowledge on the 19th of October, 2007, that there was a live issue concerning confidentiality arising from her book. And as she said, The book is simply a reflection -- pardon me, the article is simply a reflection of what I put in the book, with that one exception, and that is she took out reference to confidential decisions, perhaps because of the warning letter, thinking that that would be sufficient. There has been a fair bit of discussion and evidence concerning this notion of waiver and whether and to what extent documents and information entered into the public domain. I don't propose to go into private session, so I'll keep my comments fairly general. The detail can be found in my written brief. But at the end of the day, my submission is this: that it is clearly a doubtful proposition that an applicant for protective measures, in this case a state, can unilaterally waive any protective measures. That is a very doubtful proposition, in my submission. In addition to that, factually in this case, it's my submission that the evidence does not demonstrate any sort of waiver, whether it's express or implied, and that the documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you, sir. Is Madam Hartmann charged with revealing what the applicant in the confidential decisions sought to have protected, or is she charged with revealing the contents of the Appeal Chamber's decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: The order in lieu of indictment, in my submission, focuses on the contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And not the underlying documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would it then be -- do you find it helpful to go to that direction of the waiver? The applicant waives what he sought to have protected. The accused is not charged with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: At the end of my comments, and perhaps I could move directly to that point, it was my submission that the whole area of waiver took us off on an off-ramp, and it's irrelevant to the case. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you jumping off the off-ramp, yourself? That's my question, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: No. I felt -- I felt the need to at least address the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you want to off-ramp, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: No, I don't think it's necessary for me to do that, because for -- perhaps I could move right to the -- to my main points in relation to that, because we did spend a fair bit of time dealing with waiver and the fact that the information was in the public domain or it was alleged to be. It is my submission that, as a matter of law, that doesn't -- it's not available to an accused; secondly, it doesn't arise on the facts of this case; and, thirdly, the documents, in any event, demonstrated that there have been no waiver. So I'll just simply leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: There are a couple of cases that I feel the need to comment on because they come close to being dispositive in this particular case. One is Marijacic in 2006 from the Appeals Chamber, which holds quite simply that a court order remains in force until a Chamber decides otherwise. That's a very straightforward proposition. In my submission, it's controlling in this case. The second case that I'd like to rely upon, in part, because of this notion of information and documents being in the public domain, and we spent a fair bit of time on that, but once again the Jovic decision is directly on point, and in my submission it is dispositive of the issue. And this is the only quotation that I will be quoting to the Chamber this morning, because it is so important: "As the Trial Chamber correctly recognised, the actus reus of contempt under Rule 77 is the disclosure of information relating to proceedings before the International Tribunal --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for reading slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you: " ... where such disclosure would be in violation of an order of a Chamber. In such a case, the language of Rule 77 shows that a violation of a court order, as such, constitutes an interference with the International Tribunal's administration of justice. Any defiance of an order --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. MacFarlane. I'm told there is no French translation coming to Judge Guney's earphones. Excuse me. Okay, it's restored now. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you. "Any defiance of an order of a Chamber, per se, interferes with the administration of justice for the purposes of a conviction for contempt. No additional proof of harm to the International Tribunal's administration of justice is required." Then the next statement is critically important here: "Moreover, an order remains in force until a Chamber decides otherwise. The fact that some portions of the witness's written statement or closed-session testimony may have been disclosed to another third party does not mean that this information was no longer protected, that the court order had been de facto lifted, or that its violation would not interfere with the Tribunal's administration of justice." On that basis, there can be no other conclusion aside from the fact that the two orders, the two decisions in issue that are outlined in the order in lieu of indictment, are in -- are in force and are unaffected by they're having been leaked or emerging in some public fora. One or two comments very briefly on the evidence of Ms. Kandic. I dealt with this in a bit more detail in my written argument. Suffice it to say at this point today, given the time-limits, it's my respectful submission that the Chamber will need to examine very closely her evidence, in terms of the weight to be given to it. And I've outlined the number of times where the witness was non-responsive to questions and launched into a speech to advance her agenda. Weight is very much a live issue in connection with her evidence. On the issue of freedom of expression, which appears to be a live issue in this particular case, the leading cases, once again, are Marijacic and Jovic. In Jovic, the Trial Chamber made a finding that is quite helpful. That Chamber said: "It is undeniable that legal instruments relevant to the work of this Tribunal protect freedom of expression. All the instruments on freedom of the press have qualifications in relation to court proceedings. The Tribunal has further noted that having chosen to ignore valid orders, an accused cannot invoke the principle of freedom of expression to excuse his or her conduct." That's directly on point. If you choose to ignore a valid order, you cannot invoke the principle of freedom of expression to excuse your own conduct. There is also a decision called case of Dupuis from the European Court of Human Rights which is to the same effect. And I'll simply leave it there because it is set out in my written argument. There are limits to all rights, and particularly here the critical limitation is to ensure that the administration of justice is not frustrated by the broad application of the right to freedom of expression. The last point I would like to make, in a very summary way, is in relation to sentencing considerations, on the assumption that there is a finding of guilt, and only on that assumption. The Prosecution agrees that the accused's motives in undertaking the two publications was not reprehensible, but I've already put forward the proposition that her words are one of public defiance. Mr. Vincent, in his testimony, outlined the dangers associated with publication of state-protected information. The danger, quite simply, is that the information and the sources could dry up. The state providing them may decide, and it would be open to them, to say, I'm not going to provide any further information to the Tribunal, not if they allow these sorts of leaks and then don't enforce breaches. I set out the legislative framework for the sentencing considerations. The Chamber is well aware of them. It involves a balancing between aggravating and mitigating, and I'd like to quickly run through both sides of the coin, because there are, as usual, a number on both sides, and in fairness, I want to outline both. On the aggravating circumstances side, there were two separate and distinct publications, separated by four months. In between was the warning from the Registrar. The first one, the book, did involve a commercial venture, with a view to obtaining royalties and an advance. The accused had formerly been a senior employee of the Tribunal who knew and understood the importance of confidentiality. And, finally, the scope of the publications was significant. The first one was a book issued by a major publisher in France. The second was placed on the internet for the world to see. On the mitigating circumstances side, and I'm sure that my learned friend will have more to say on this, but I want to be fair and outline my perception of mitigating circumstances, I do want to indicate to the Chamber that the accused did cooperate during the course of the investigation and allowed herself to be interviewed on two separate occasions in her counsel's office. The second point is that the distribution of the first publication, her book, was more limited than perhaps she wanted. The book was not successful. Her motives were not reprehensible, as I mentioned. The accused is a mother of two children. And while this is not evidence, has not the subject of admission with -- or even discussion with counsel. The Prosecution wishes to advise the Chamber that to the best our knowledge, the accused has not previously been charged or convicted with anything. And, finally -- I'll leave it at that. It's my respectful submission that based on the facts in this case, and the mitigating --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your 30 minutes are actually over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I can do this in 15 seconds, if that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you. It's my respectful submission that a term of imprisonment is not called for, would not be justified, and that the issue is a monetary penalty, and the issue is quantum. I've set out the cases in my written argument. It's my respectful submission that a fine in the vicinity of 7.000 to 15.000 Euros would be appropriate and consistent with previous decisions of the Chamber. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, it seems a while back, when this case started, and in the opening remarks that I put before Your Honours for their consideration, I mentioned that one of the distinctive features of this case, in my respectful submission, was the constant erosion that there has been in the Prosecution's assertions. In this regard, Your Honours, I do ask you to look at the report that the amicus investigator put before the originally-composed, specially-appointed Trial Chamber. That provides some context, a background tapestry, if you will, for the genesis of these proceedings. And what struck me, Your Honours, is the number of very general allegations that are made that have not been the subject of evidence. In some systems, of course, it is normal that at committal hearings individuals, whose names are detailed on the back of an indictment, are required to attend. Your Honours, I'm not going to go into the confidential report in detail, but what I will say is I would ask Your Honours to consider it and look at the gap between what was alleged therein in relation to the policy of the Prosecution, an attempt to deflect attention and criticism onto the Bench, and actually what arose at trial itself. This erosion continued, in my respectful submission, even in the pre-trial brief. If Your Honours refer in due course to the pre-trial brief of my learned friend on the 8th of January, 2009, it will not escape Your Honours' attention at all that a number of averments are made, regarding which there has not been a scintilla of evidence put forward by the learned amicus prosecutor. He states, for example, that my client was a chief of staff, a chef de cabinet, a principle policy advisor of Carla Del Ponte. Not a word has been spoken or a sentence submitted to Your Honours that would support such a sweeping assertion, which is utterly devoid of merit and is singularly unsupported by the case that my learned friend has put before you. A pre-trial brief is not a redundant document. It is the Prosecution's view of his own case, and he has failed, hasn't even attempted to adduce evidence in support of these completely unmeritorious allegations. It is evidence, in our respectful submission, of a desperate attempt by my learned friend to seek to get a conviction in this case, regardless of the reality of what took place and the conduct of my client. In short and to put it bluntly, it smacks of desperation. Your Honours, the other aspect is the rather perplexing, in my respectful submission, or most quixotic selection of witnesses that my learned friend has chosen to put before you. The nature of these witnesses highlights, in my respectful submission, an underlying weakness in the Prosecution's case, fundamental misconceptions. And who he does not call is equally pertinent. His very first witness was Kermarrec, and as Mr. Kermarrec answered to the insightful comment of Judge Guney, Mr. Kermarrec fully accepted from Flammarion Publishers that he didn't sign the contact with Florence Hartmann, he wasn't part of the negotiations with Florence Hartmann. Indeed, he specifies that Giles Haeri is the person who did that, and yet Giles Haeri is not called before Your Honours to explain the negotiations of the contract, what was agreed; but Mr. Kermarrec. Mr. Vincent, of course, Robin Vincent, was the second witness. Now, he was to give -- and of course we didn't have the benefit of statements, but he was to give a general overview as to the need, in abstract terms, of the need of confidentiality, and of course he added some flesh to that assertion when he gave evidence. But what are the charges? It is highly important, and Your Honours cannot turn away from it easily, in my respectful submission, that the Prosecution, charged with the conduct of this case, responsible for its investigation, has failed to call anybody from the applicant state, Serbia, on whose behest the very confidentiality of the decisions was predicated. Neither did he attempt to call them as witness, nor did he obtain a statement from them, nor is there any evidence whatsoever in any form, rumour, newspaper, press reports, that the applicant state, Serbia, was at any time in the least troubled by the book written by my client. There is no evidence at all to support the fact that Serbia viewed the book and the article written by Ms. Hartmann as in any way encroaching upon the decision that they asked to be made confidential. Your Honours, this is important for a number of reasons, and I'll touch only upon one. It is relevant, because what it discloses is the parameters of what was viewed as confidential. Serbia, itself, and this is the uncontested evidence of Natasa Kandic, it's been the subject of litigation in the International Court of Justice, all these matters have been gone into at some length in my opening and during the course of examinations of the witnesses. But Serbia, itself, alluded to the fact that these decisions that the ICTY had been seized of a case, seized of an application, that it referred to confidential decisions, that it related to the SDC documents, and certain portions had been redacted. Now, what is so unusual in the book written by my client that would merit the stigma and punishment and chilling effect of a criminal conviction for a woman of previously exceptional character, in my submission? There is no good reason. Once again, my learned friend's position may or may not have evolved; I couldn't quite grasp it. But he said in his opening that actus reus was not in dispute, and in my response, I said, well, it is very much in dispute; it is one of the core elements that we take issue with. And also he made the comment, very much as an aside, as it were, that this case is not about the rights of journalists. In fact, if one looks at the opening, it will not escape Your Honours' attention that much more time is spent by my learned friend about what this case is not about than actually what it is about. But going to the actus reus, the client -- the amicus prosecutor has said that this case is about four key issues, and he talks about actus reus and mens rea. And then again in his third and fourth points, to me, Your Honours, and I may be wrong, he again repeats what were the first two elements, actus reus and mens rea. But the way he put his case, and to date, there has not been any contradiction by my learned friend in relation to the Defence understanding, what is being treated as confidential by the Tribunal is the existence and date of the two impugned decisions, the confidential character of these decisions, the identity of the moving party and the applicants, and, fourthly, the subject; namely, that the protective measures were granted in relation to the SDC minutes. And, Your Honours, we made this -- we clarified our position in our motion for reconsideration on the 9th of January, 2009, repeated it on the 14th of January, 2009. We placed that understanding in our pre-trial brief, and it was stated by me in my opening. And there has been no dissent, in my respectful submission, from the amicus prosecutor in relation to this position. Now, what my learned friend states, of course, is that he has prepared a line-by-line analysis in relation to those two pages, page 122 and 123 of Florence Hartmann's book and tied it in to the allegations that he must prove. Your Honours, as I am standing here speaking to Your Honours, I have not had the benefit of reading that closing brief. Leaving that aside, I would ask Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Khan, I've been listening to the French booth. I must say that the interpreter is suffering a lot and is finding it difficult to follow. You are speaking extremely fast. Please slow down to enable the interpreters to do a proper job and to enable us also to understand what your train of thought is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm most grateful. I will endeavour to be even slower. I was endeavouring to keep my eye on the English transcript, and I do apologise to our colleagues that are labouring sisyphusly to translate my utterances into French. Your Honour, in understanding the parameters of this case, the views of the applicant state are not a side issue. They are very far removed from an off-ramp that my learned friend would seek to characterise them as. The Appeals Chamber has made it clear that what was the subject of protective measures in this case were the SDC minutes and the stenographic notes, and that's detailed in the Milosevic decision of the 11th of September, 2007. The Appeals Chamber has similarly explained that the confidential status granted to a decision is, and I quote, "in relation to confidential information noted therein for which the protective measures have been ordered under the Rules." Your Honours, when one is looking at the view of Serbia, when one is reviewing what they said about these decisions and their own applications before the Appeals Chamber of this Tribunal, it is pertinent to bear in mind that what their primary concern was, in my respectful submission, their only concern, it was to prevent the underlying documents which would prejudice their case in the International Court of Justice from entering the public domain. This is why both in the International Court of Justice and in the roundtable discussion that Natasa Kandic refers to, they draw this fundamental distinction between the underlying documents and the fact of an application, the subject matter of the application, or the confidentiality of a decision. Your Honour, I'm not going to go into detail on this issue because it is dealt with at some length in our pre-trial brief, but of paramount importance, when one is viewing the actus reus and whether or not it has been made out, Your Honours cannot readily ignore the practice of various Chambers of this Court. We made the submission in our pre-trial brief and in our opening that by way of actus contrarius, Benches of this Court can vary the nature of decisions in a number of ways. That averment has not been contradicted by my learned friend for the Prosecution. Indeed, it was his own witness, Robin Vincent, who accepted that reality in cross-examination. Repeatedly, Mr. Vincent made it clear that the nature of a decision could be varied in a number of ways. And Your Honours will just have to look at the transcript. On three separate occasions during his cross-examination, he was shown documents and he accepted that documents could be rendered confidential, absent a written decision of a Trial Chamber or Appeals Chamber by way of their practice. And we cited in our opening Your Honour Judge Moloto's own practice in this very case as an example of the way in which what had been rendered confidential, how it could be clarified, the status could evolve, by way of judicial practice, and how a Bench, in public session, treated a decision. And we've detailed that previously. I hope that the point is clear. Your Honour, if you'll just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the transcript in that regard will speak for itself. I can go into more detail, should that be needed. The Prosecution has failed absolutely to address the mens rea aspect of this case. They would have Your Honours adopt what I can only describe as some kind of legal fundamentalism, that where a decision is entitled "Confidential," any reference to it would give rise to criminal liability for contempt. The extract in Jovic, I think it was, that my learned friend cited in his opening had to do totally with the actus reus of the offence, not the mens rea, but when one is putting oneself in the shoes of the accused, who Your Honours will judge in due course, Your Honours will be alive to the fact that everything she wrote was in the public domain. Now, it is, of course, accepted that the simple fact that something is in the public domain is not dispositive. It doesn't mean just because a fact is in the public domain, there is a license for any individual to repeat it with abandon. But that is not to say that the fact that a decision is in the public domain is irrelevant. To make that quantum leap would be exactly that, a quantum leap that is not justified in law or in logic. In contradistinction to the various cases, indeed all the cases that have come before Your Honours and other Chambers of this Tribunal, this case did not involve disclosure of a witness's name. That, of course, would be the matter of the highest concern to a Bench because it could jeopardise their life. This book that is the subject of proceedings, and the article that followed it, had been all in the public domain for years. Your Honours were taken at some length by my learned friend Mr. Mettraux to the International War and Peace report -- special report in 2005, when all these facts were made public. The horse had bolted. Of course, that was prior to a decision, but the fact that these issues were already in the public domain must be factored in when one is seeking to identify what interest it is that the Appeals Chamber was seeking to protect. Six months before her book was published, another report appeared in the Institute of War and Peace Reporting, talking about the Appeals Chamber's decision, and it was followed by reports in "The New York Times" and the "International Herald Tribune," newspapers of world fame, fantastic circulation. And as I mentioned in the opening, and unfortunately I cannot put it better, there was not a whisper or a murmur from the corridors of the Registry. No Rule 33 submission was filed, no public statement was made. These issues were being discussed in Belgrade, they were being discussed in New York, they were being discussed by the Institute of War and Peace Reporting, and how could a reasonable individual, looking at that, consider that saying the same things, discussing the same matters, would give rise to criminal responsibility? We have gone into detail about other individuals who have been employees of this Court that have said similar things. No action taken against them. Your Honour, this is relevant to mens rea. However my learned friend seeks to get 'round it, and the way he gets 'round it is by not addressing it, it is relevant to mens rea. There is no guilty mind by my client. As Natasa Kandic put it very clearly, that before she was employed by the Tribunal, she was committed and knowledgeable and an expert in the former Yugoslavia. Indeed, she was an individual -- Ms. Hartmann was the individual that in many ways inspired Natasa Kandic to start the work she started. Now, my learned friend may wish to characterise her evidence as one of giving speeches. Your Honours will decide that. But she is a woman of enormous renown, not just because the "Times," in 2002, named her one of the people of the year, or that in 2007 she was declared one of the heroes of the last 60 years, but because of the work she's done and, more importantly, because of what she knows is the situation on the ground in the former Yugoslavia. As she put it very eloquently, she could not believe how Florence Hartmann could be sitting in that seat for writing about nothing remarkable, simply writing in a book with a circulation of 3.000 only on a topic that had been discussed in detail in Belgrade and in international papers. In deciding whether or not a criminal offence has been committed, one must contrast this case with the actions of the authorities of this Court, be they the Prosecution or the Registry, in their supervisory role in relation to issues of confidentiality, or their policing role, not supervisory, their policing role, to the other cases like Haxhiu. In all those cases, there was no gap to speak of between an alleged breach coming to light and action by the Tribunal. Here we have years -- 2005, the facts had been in the public domain, and six months in which newspapers had been talking -- speaking about these issues. These are relevant considerations for Your Honour, and they are matters that need the most careful scrutiny. Your Honour, the other factor the Prosecution fails to address is this: All cases of contempt previously have related to live cases. This case, at the time the alleged contempt was committed, had ceased. He doesn't address this at all. In fact, I noticed, and I stand to be corrected from the transcript, but he didn't address at all the aspect that is most important to mens rea, an intention of Ms. Hartmann to interfere with the administration of justice. Rather Janus-faced, perhaps, he says, Well, she doesn't act out of reprehensible motives, and at the same time, of course, he is seeking to say that there is a guilty mind. Well, Your Honour, there hasn't been an intent to interfere with the administration of justice. The proceedings were dead, there was no specific intent, and indeed such a specific intent needs to be proved, a knowing or willful intent to interfere in the administration of justice. Now, what did the Beqaj Trial Chamber say? My learned friend states, well, these cases he cites as dispositive, yet there is no mention of cases that are contradictory to the submission that he puts forward. Well, Beqaj says that there must be proof, and I quote: " ... of a specific intent to interfere with the administration of justice. Thus," and I quote, "the mens rea of contempt is the knowledge and the will to interfere with the administration of justice." The Maglov case, the Maglov decision is in our brief, and I quote: "The Prosecution must establish that the accused had the specific intent to interfere with the Tribunal's administration of justice. In the South African case, the State and van Nieckert, I believe, Mr. President, that may be the leading case in South Africa, that the Court stated, and I quote: "Before a conviction for contempt can result, the act complained of must not only be willful and calculated to bring into contempt, but also be made with the intention of bringing the Judges, in their judicial capacity, into contempt, or casting suspicion on the administration of justice." Your Honours, therefore, I would invite Your Honours to askew a mechanical application of the law, what I described as legal fundamentalism, that any violation, as such, automatically amounts to an interference --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you considering that there has been a violation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, not at all. My preliminary remark is that there's no actus reus. That was my first primary submission, and the reason for that was the actus contrarius and also the waiver by the state which will delineate that. But as far as the amicus's submission is concerned, it's a very rigid view that a decision is entitled confidential. And if it's revealed, not only is the actus reus made out, and that was the authority he cited, the actus reus, but also there's an interference with the administration of justice. Now, this is a preposterous submission. Your Honours will look at the various cases we've discussed in our motions and the various decisions I put to Robin Vincent. All of those decisions, we constrained ourselves. All the jurisprudence related to the two impugned decisions. They all related to the two decisions subject to the case against Ms. Hartmann. But if Your Honours reviewed the totality of the jurisprudence of this Court, even one or two cases, Your Honours would come to the inescapable conclusion that it is replete with examples where confidential decisions are referred to in public session; not just the title, not just the name, not just the existence of a decision, but the jurisprudence. And, Your Honour, we have shown that, even in relation to the two impugned decisions or the two decisions that are subjects of these proceedings, when I put questions to Robin Vincent and we read out from public decisions the exact quotations and the exact jurisprudence from -- in public session from the decisions that Ms. Hartmann is alleged to have spoken about criminally, in criminal breach of the contempt provisions. As I said, Your Honours, the amicus focuses solely on the fact that the heading of these decisions was "Confidential," and, therefore, comes to the conclusion that, therefore, if it's filed confidentially, a breach must have taken place. Your Honour, the other aspect that hasn't really been addressed is the issue of mistake of law or of fact. Now, my learned friend has referred to this warning letter from the Registrar, and I can't pass that topic without expressing my extreme disquiet at the conduct of my learned friend in this regard. It is a matter of significant disappointment, Your Honours, that without giving any good reason, the Prosecutor charged with the conduct of this case, who has a duty under Article 15 of the Practice Direction not to prosecute adversarially, but to prosecute in an impartial manner, that he should renege upon a written undertaking to counsel. And Your Honours, of course, made a ruling, but it's an issue that has to be addressed in relation to the fairness to the Defence, the bid -- and my learned friend has said quite openly, Ms. Hartmann cannot escape. These were his words. Individuals -- no one can escape. Your Honours, this is not the role of a prosecutor, to try to avoid escape. The role of a prosecutor is to put the facts before a Bench and then for the Bench to decide if the actus reus and mens rea are made out. But when we asked for the chain of custody in relation to this document that he now relies upon, his answer was, Well, no, I'm not going to rely upon it in my case in-chief. If I rely upon it at all, it will be in cross-examination, and therefore your request regarding the chain of custody is irrelevant. Now, when I stood up in a matter of candour to the Court, without keeping things under my ample sleeves, I made it clear that I didn't have an intention of calling Florence Hartmann. Right at the end, before he sought to close his case, he reneged on that promise, and this is a matter of concern. It hasn't been explained away, other than the fact that we had the document. It's simply not good enough. It's not how a case should have been prosecuted at all. Your Honour, my learned friend has spoken repeatedly about off-ramps, but with the greatest of respect, to choose another metaphor, he has not been slow at all to lead you on highways and byways in order to find a way to convict. Your Honour, it's not your role, and Your Honours don't need any guidance from me in that regard - perish the thought - but of course it's not the role of a Court or of a prudent prosecutor to find a way to convict, to avoid somebody to escape. The principle of in dubio pro reo applies. And we did have significant concerns regarding the motivations of this case. We have tried, and it's a matter of context, to have hearings regarding an abuse of process. It was denied. We sought to question the investigating officer in this case, who happened to be -- who happens to be now the prosecutor. That was denied. Your Honours have been prevented from getting beneath -- looking at the skull beneath the skin of this case and looking at the motivations. Like cases must be treated alike. Not rocket science, not another proposition. And the cases my learned friend puts to you are not alike. The issue of revealing a witness's name is fundamentally different from discussing, in a democratic, pluralistic, international community the jurisprudence and reasoning of a bench of Judges. The cases my learned friend cites all have to deal with cases where the applicant, the protected person, the witness, never sought to reveal their own name. In this case, the applicant is making no bones about the fact that an application has been made. Speaking at roundtable conferences, speaking at the ICJ. The matter has been discussed on the radio in Belgrade. It's the subject of TV reports. Fundamentally different to the cases cited by my learned friend. Like cases should be treated alike. No action in relation to the "The New York Times", the "International Herald Tribune," the Institute of war and Peace Reporting. Your Honours must have pause for thought and ask why is Florence Hartmann being targeted. The amicus prosecutor, in his opening, said something along the lines of, This is not about whether or not Florence Hartmann deserves special treatment as a former employee of this Court. The converse is also true, Your Honours. Ms. Hartmann does not merit special targeting, particular targeting, simply because she happened to be a servant of this Tribunal for six years. She should not be singled out, when all these other entities, editors, newspapers, and other lawyers have done exactly that, with no reaction. That, itself, is relevant not only to the principle of like cases being treated alike, but whether or not an offence was committed at all. And it goes back, of course, to her mens rea. A reasonable person, looking at that state of affairs, would they consider that the article and the book written by Florence Hartmann would be contemptuous? In my respectful submission, no reasonable person would come to such a conclusion. Your Honours, my learned friend seeks to escape or gloss over, at the very least, the welter of international human rights law. In fact, some of the very cases he cites as dispositive are absolutely against him. Now, he -- my learned friend could castigate Natasa Kandic as being -- giving speeches and pursuing an agenda, despite the fact that this lady, the recipient of numerous awards, of good character, was giving evidence under oath. But, Your Honours, at least my learned friend has not sought to castigate or colour the testimony of Mr. Joinet, one of the leading world experts and somebody intimately familiar with the factors and considerations in relation to freedom of expression, a man that has been honoured to serve six French prime ministers. What did he say, Your Honours, in his questioning on the 16th of June? He said he had never been aware of a case of contempt which was focused on the reasoning of a Trial Chamber or an Appeals Chamber being revealed. So my learned friend would ask you to turn away from the accumulated case law of Strasbourg, and in order to take you on his merry dance towards the conviction that he wishes you to reach, be totally blind to the fact that no other courts that he is aware of has found an individual guilty in these circumstances of something similar. The reason, in my respectful submission, such individuals have not -- such courts have not found somebody guilty in similar circumstances is because the offence simply is not made out. And the error is not that of all the other courts. Let's stick to Europe for the time being. It's not the fault of Strasbourg or domestic courts in Europe; the fault is the fundamental misapprehension of the law of contempt of this Tribunal by the amicus prosecutor brought in to conduct this investigation and this case. Your Honours, I will touch upon three decisions, the last of which -- or the second of which is Dupuis which my friend relied upon. But in the "Sunday Times" case, it's the "Sunday Times" and the United Kingdom, the 1979 case, the Court made it clear that freedom of expression has a pivotal role in society, and whilst, of course, it is a qualified right, it is not an absolute right. It is clear from all the case studies, both by the United Nations that Mr. Joinet referred to and the case law at Strasbourg, that any restrictions on freedom of expression must be interpreted narrowly. This is the starting point. The presumption is in favour of freedom of expression. The presumption is against restriction. Now, in the "Sunday Times" case, this had to do with thalidomide and the awful effects of that drug on children. Strasbourg said, and I quote from page 61: "In the present case, the families of numerous victims of the tragedy who were unaware of the legal difficulties involved had a vital interest in knowing all the underlying facts and the various possible solutions. They could be deprived of this information, which was crucially important to them, only if it appeared that its diffusion would have presented a threat to the authority of the judiciary." Now, Your Honours will see from my closing brief that there is ample case law stating that the judiciary and the rule of law is robust enough to take care of itself. The law of contempt is not there to buttress the dignity of the Judges. It is not there to save any blushes of any judicial institution. It is there to safe-guard the administration of justice. And whilst it's correct that the administration of justice does not have to be shown to have been impeded, it must be established that there is an intent to so impede. It is this intent to impede the administration of justice that has been absolutely not proved by the amicus prosecutor. Your Honour, you will see from our brief and the book of authorities an awful lot of -- the highlighted cases, extracts of the various cases, and I would urge Your Honours in due course to give particularly -- particular care when reading these. It will take a little bit of time, but hopefully they are instructive on this issue. Your Honour, in assessing the -- whether or not the restrictions on freedom of expression are needed, the Prosecution must establish that the law, as he intends it to apply, fulfils a pressing social need, that it is proportionate, and this issue of proportionality is absolutely fundamental. Your Honour, in the same case, and I'll read, Strasbourg European Court of Human Rights held that: "There is a general recognition --" Let me start again: "As the Court remarked in its Handyside judgement, freedom of expression constitutes one of the essential foundations of a democratic society." It goes on to say: "It is applicable not only to information or ideas that are favorably received, or regarded as inoffensive, or as a matter of indifference, but also to those that shock, offend, or disturb the state or any sector of the population. These principles are of particular importance as far as the press is concerned." I pause there. My learned friend's opening remarks, of course, seem to diminish any different standard, any different considerations, when one is dealing with journalists and journalistic freedom. That has been rejected by the European Court of Human Rights. A margin of deference is given to journalists in democratic, pluralistic societies, consistent with the principles of the European Court of Human Rights. But whilst this may seem Eurocentric, Your Honours, these principles have found voice in many other international conventions that were alluded to by Professor Joinet in his testimony. The Court continued: "These principles are equally applicable to the field of the administration of justice which serves the interests of the community at large and requires the cooperation," "requires the cooperation," "of an enlightened public. There is general recognition of the fact that the courts cannot operate in a vacuum. Whilst they are the forum for the settlement of disputes, this does not mean that there can be no prior discussion of disputes elsewhere, be it in specialised journals, in the general press, or amongst the public at large. "Furthermore, whilst the mass media must not over-step the bounds imposed in the proper administration of justice, it is incumbent upon them," it is incumbent upon them, a burden of the press, Strasbourg is saying, "to impart information and ideas concerning matters that come before the courts, just as in other areas of public interest." Not only do the media have the task of imparting that knowledge; the public have the right to receive it. And it states that the restrictions must be narrowly interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Khan, we have gone as far as the tape can take us. We've gone for one and a half hours. You are actually left with nine minutes to finish your brief. We just have to take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm most grateful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am most grateful. Your Honour, in the short amount of time left, I will seek to focus on just three issues and rest, then, on the closing brief that is before Your Honours. The first issue is one of clarification, perhaps. We wish to be clear that we are not challenging, in any way, shape, or form, the legality of the appropriateness or the legal foundations of the Appeals Chamber's two decisions that gave rise to this case. Of course, being an apex court, being an apex judge, is never easy. It is more often the case -- more often the case than not that one litigant, one party or the other, will be dissatisfied with the verdicts that are meted out. Your Honours, in determining this case, you do not need to find at all -- make any finding at all as to the legality or the appropriateness of those two decisions. What you are simply tasked to focus on is whether or not the elements of contempt are made out. In determining that, Your Honours must consider whether or not my learned friend for the Prosecution has discharged his onerous burden to prove this case beyond reasonable doubt. In establishing the ingredients of this offence, it is our hopefully clear submission that the Prosecution must establish that the conduct of Ms. Hartmann gave rise to a real risk -- a real risk to the administration of justice. Unless such a risk exists, it is our submission that the Tribunal has no jurisdiction. This is because the contempt jurisdiction of this Court does not stand alone. It is there under its implied powers to support the functioning of the Court. Your Honours, I will refer, and it's in our brief, to the Margetic Trial Chamber decision at paragraph 15, and also the Marijacic Trial Chamber decision at paragraph 50. Now, Your Honours, this "real risk" test has not even been -- has not just been referred to by your brethren and sister Judges in this court; it find origins in those system that have been tasked to deal with contempt provisions for decades. Your Honours, the real risk to the prejudice to the administration of justice has, and I'm quoting: "Has, since the European Court of Human Rights era, always -- always been used in relation to particular proceedings, not in relation to the administration of justice generally." So says Fenwick and Phillipson, which happens to be the leading text in one jurisdiction, namely that of England and Wales. That has been echoed by Mr. Joinet when he stated that when the case is over, there is no problem regarding the administration of justice. So in this focus of mischief, what is the mischief that the Rule is tendered to focus on? It is my submission -- it is our submission that the civil law and the common law stand shoulder to shoulder that this ingredient of real risk must be made out. Your Honour, there are many cases referred to in our closing brief, but let me just read, by way of, hopefully, to illuminate the issue to some extent, the finding of Lord Bridge in the House of Lords in the Lonrho case, a famous case in England and Wales, and His Lordship said, and I quote at page 209 of that judgement: "Whether the course of justice in particular proceedings will be impeded or prejudiced by a publication must depend primarily on whether the publication will bring influence to bear which is likely to divert the proceedings in some way from the course that they would otherwise have followed. The influence may affect the conduct of the witness, the parties, or the Court." No such risk has been made out in the present case. Your Honours, I've already referred to the fact that there's been no evidence at all called by the Prosecutor in an attempt to discharge his burden of proof from the applicant state, but, Your Honours, you've also had put before you earlier this week evidence from the Prosecutor of this Court stating that cooperation from that applicant state, Serbia, has improved since the book was published. So there's absolutely no real risk at all that has been shown by the amicus prosecutor. Going to the Dupuis case, it is surprising - surprising is the word I would use - that my learned friend seeks to rely upon it. And I would ask Your Honours to rely upon it because it kicks his case into touch. Your Honours, I will refer to only one paragraph of that case, paragraph 46. It's in our -- an extract is in our book of authorities at page 18. And what the European Court of Human Rights found, and I quote: "The Court further considers that it is necessary to take the greatest care in assessing the need, in a democratic society, to punish journalists for using information obtained through a breach of the secrecy of an investigation, or a breach of professional confidence, when those journalists are contributing to a public debate of such importance and are thereby playing their role as watch-dogs of democracy. Article 10 protects the rights of journalists to divulge information on issues of public interest, provided they are acting in good faith and on an accurate factual basis, and provide reliable and precise information in accordance with the ethics of journalism." You now, Your Honours, my learned friend has stated he doesn't seek incarceration -- I'll be four minutes, Your Honour. My learned friend states --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your four minutes are gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could have four minutes to conclude, and I'll be as quick as I can. I would be most grateful. My learned friend has stated he doesn't seek to incarcerate my client, but, Your Honours, in that case the European Court held that whilst there'd been no order to destroy or seize the book that had been published, whilst a sentence of imprisonment was not ordered, the fine that was imposed had a chilling effect and therefore constituted a disproportionate interference with the right of freedom of expression. Your Honours, the last case, pivotal case, is the case of Weber and Switzerland. I'll read one paragraph which debunks the theory that my learned friend would have you adopt, the legal fundamentalist position that he would ramrod to Your Honours. There, Strasbourg Court, dismissing the position of the Swiss government, and I quote, the Strasbourg European Court states: "In the government submission, this finding was not decisive because of the formal nature of the confidentiality. According to the relevant Swiss case law and legal literature, the mere fact of communicating a piece of information in a judicial investigation was sufficient for the commission of an offence. Whether it was common knowledge beforehand, and its importance, or its degree of confidentiality, they were relative to the fine." That position is identical -- materially identical to the position advanced by my learned friend, the amicus prosecutor. Strasbourg rejected it totally. The European Court stated: "The Court finds this submission unpersuasive. For the purposes of the convention, the interest in maintaining the confidentiality of the aforementioned facts no longer existed in March 1982. On that date, therefore, the penalty imposed on the applicant no longer appeared necessary in order to achieve the legitimate aim pursued." And therefore they had regard to the circumstance and concluded that the conviction and the fine was not necessary in a democratic society. Your Honour, these proceedings have taken a while, they have led to the disqualification of one Bench. They have led to numerous motions being filed. It may well be thought in some quarters that the Defence have been leading you up off-ramps. Your Honours will be the determiners of. But I would caution Your Honours from adopting a view that simply because an individual states in a book a decision is confidential, a conviction will follow. Going back to Vincent, Christiane Amanpour referred to an incident, didn't say it was confidential. That surely cannot be the pivotal issue that will give rise to a conviction, whether or not a book states such and such a decision is confidential or not. For the reasons we have sought to put before you, it is our submission that the actus reus and the mens rea of this offence -- of these two counts are not made out. To the extent that any of our submissions may have been viewed as being robust, Your Honours, we have considered it, Mr. Mettraux and ourselves, necessary to do our best to persuade Your Honours to have pause for thought, not just to jump a step to a conviction that my learned friend thinks is certain and an irresistible conclusion. To the extent that we have done anything wrong, we would ask, of course, that Ms. Hartmann not be penalised by the way that we have sought to defend her interests. And, Your Honours, we are confident, of course, that that will not be the case. As far as the letter is concerned -- this is my final point. As far as the Rule 77 letter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's my last point. As far as the letter is concerned and from the Registry, I will only say that that letter did not refer to Rule 77, it did not refer to contempt or the two impugned decisions. The amicus prosecutor, himself, has conceded that Ms. Hartmann did not see these two decisions until the time she was interviewed by him. And in my respectful submission, from that interview her reaction at the time was that these -- that letter had nothing to do with the two decisions that are subject of these proceedings. For all of these reasons, it is my respectful submission that Ms. Hartmann -- that Ms. Hartmann must be acquitted, and Your Honours should resist any attempt by the amicus prosecutor to lead you to an alternative conclusion that would have a chilling effect on freedom of speech, the rights of victims, and those that wish to engage and uphold the principles espoused in Security Council Resolution 827, which is the foundational instrument that led to the creation of this Tribunal. Your Honour, those are my submissions, unless I can assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Khan. I think the parties will hear from the Chamber. The matter stands adjourned. Court adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.16 a.m.
